passage: The day I quit the café, I didn't plan it. The manager snapped at me for being two minutes late, in front of customers, and I pulled off my apron, dropped it on the counter and walked out. I'm Manoj, twenty, and for about an hour I felt amazing, like a film hero. Then I remembered the rent was due in nine days. My friend Pranav let me sleep on his floor for a month while I looked for work. He didn't lecture. He just said, "Next time you're that angry, text me before you do anything. Give it one night." I've done that twice since. Both times, by morning, I'd found a better way.

qa.q: How many days were left before the rent was due?
qa.a: Nine days.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel right after walking out, and later?
qa.a: Manoj felt amazing, like a film hero, for about an hour, then worried and regretful about the rent.

qa.q: What habit did Pranav suggest, and why does it help?
qa.a: Texting Pranav and giving it one night before acting, which lets the anger cool before a big decision.

qa.q: What is it like for Pranav to have Manoj on his floor for a month?
qa.a: Pranav is patient and supportive, choosing to help rather than lecture.

grounding: Shows a young adult who quits a job in anger, faces the cost and builds a delay habit with a friend's support.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Tuesday. Disha, second year, came in upset. On Friday, after a fight with her boyfriend, she ended the relationship by text within ten minutes. On Saturday, still buzzing, she spent most of the month's hostel allowance on concert tickets and a jacket. By Monday she regretted both and was getting through the month on instant noodles. She said, "In the moment it feels so right. Then it's gone." We talked about a delay habit: when a big feeling hits, write the decision down and wait until the next evening before acting. She also agreed to tell her parents about the money this week, and we have booked a follow-up.
Ujjwal

qa.q: What did Disha spend the allowance on?
qa.a: Concert tickets and a jacket.

qa.q: How did Disha feel by Monday?
qa.a: She felt regret about both the break-up text and the spending.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor and Disha agree on?
qa.a: A delay habit of waiting until the next evening before acting, telling her parents about the money and a follow-up session.

qa.q: How might Disha's boyfriend have felt getting a break-up text within ten minutes?
qa.a: He was probably shocked and hurt by how sudden it was.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who ends a relationship and spends her allowance in a flash, then builds a delay habit with support.

passage:
Friday, 1 a.m. I broke up with Samir tonight. Over a missed call. He was at his cousin's engagement with his phone in his bag, and I sat in the café getting angrier and angrier, and when he finally called back I said, "You know what, we're done." And hung up. And blocked him. It felt powerful for about fifteen minutes. Now I'm lying here with my heart racing, and I don't even know if I meant it. This is the third big thing I've done in a flash this year: the course I dropped, the haircut, and now this. Didi says I should make a rule: no big decisions after 10 p.m. I think I'll unblock him in the morning and ask to talk. Not tonight.
Parul

qa.q: Where was Samir when Parul called?
qa.a: At his cousin's engagement, with his phone in his bag.

qa.q: How does Parul feel lying awake after the break-up?
qa.a: Parul feels anxious and unsure, heart racing, not knowing if it was meant.

qa.q: What rule did Didi suggest, and how might it help?
qa.a: No big decisions after 10 p.m., so strong feelings can settle before Parul acts.

qa.q: How might Samir feel on finding himself blocked?
qa.a: Samir is probably confused and hurt, having only missed a call during a family event.

grounding: Shows a young adult ending a relationship in a flash of anger and planning a delay rule to avoid regret.

passage: In the village near Sangli, Rekha heard the tractor before she saw it: Kiran, her husband, driving a second-hand one into the yard, grinning. "Got it cheap at the fair! We'll pay the loan off in two harvests." Her stomach dropped. Last year it was the motorbike; before that, the borewell he started and abandoned. She wanted to shout, to call him a fool in front of the neighbours. She didn't. That night, after the children slept, she said, "I'm scared, Kiran. These big buys happen without us talking. From now on, anything that needs a loan, we decide together." He went quiet. "And I want us to see the bank's farm adviser this week about this loan." He nodded slowly. "Together," he said.

qa.q: What did Kiran buy at the fair?
qa.a: A second-hand tractor.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel when she saw the tractor?
qa.a: Her stomach dropped; she felt scared and angry after years of sudden buys.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that avoided contempt and still set a limit?
qa.a: She waited until night, spoke calmly about her fear, asked to decide loans together and to see the farm adviser.

qa.q: How might Kiran feel when Rekha says she's scared?
qa.a: Kiran may feel surprised and sobered, seeing the worry behind her words, which is why he agrees.

grounding: Illustrates a spouse anxious about repeated rash purchases who proposes calm shared rules and professional guidance.

passage: Tuan and Bilal had run their food truck in Melbourne for two years, and Tuan had learned to dread Bilal's Monday texts. "Bought a second fryer!" "Signed us up for the festival in Perth!" Each time the shared account dipped, and Tuan lay awake doing sums. This Monday it was a new logo, already printed on five hundred cups. Tuan felt the familiar knot in his chest, and a sharp urge to say something cutting. He waited until they'd closed up. "Bil, I love working with you. And I'm anxious all the time about money. Can we agree that any big spend needs both of us to say yes first?" Bilal rubbed his neck. "I get excited." "I know. Maybe we see an accountant together and set it up properly." Bilal nodded. "Fair."

qa.q: How many cups had the new logo been printed on?
qa.a: Five hundred cups.

qa.q: How does Tuan feel after Bilal's Monday texts?
qa.a: Tuan feels anxious and tense, lying awake doing sums.

qa.q: Why was Tuan's way of raising it effective?
qa.a: He waited till closing, spoke warmly without contempt, proposed a shared rule and suggested an accountant.

qa.q: How does Bilal see his own sudden choices?
qa.a: Bilal admits he gets excited and agrees the plan is fair.

grounding: Shows a business partner anxious about sudden spending who calmly agrees rules for big decisions and suggests professional help.

passage: On the rattling bus to Nani's village, Bhupen asked, "Are we there yet?" for the ninth time. When his mother, Rajni, said the sweets from the bus stand would wait till Nani's house, he burst into tears and kicked the seat. Rajni didn't scold. "Let's count buffaloes. When we see ten, we'll be at the big banyan tree, and after that it's only one song till Nani's." Bhupen sniffed and pressed his face to the window. "One! Two!" At ten he shouted, and Rajni began the song. He sang along, wiping his nose.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen burst into tears?

qa.q: How did Rajni make the waiting easier?
qa.a: She turned it into a counting game and a song, so Bhupen could see the wait getting shorter.

qa.q: What is it like for Rajni to hear the same question nine times?
qa.a: Rajni is probably tired, but she stays patient and finds a game instead of scolding.

grounding: Shows a young child who cries over a delayed treat and repeats "are we there yet", helped by a parent's counting game and song.

passage: Dalia's fifth-birthday cake wouldn't be ready until eleven, and at breakfast in their Cairo flat she was already wailing. "I want it NOW!" They sang the birthday song twice. Dalia checked the timer every few minutes, bouncing on her toes. When it finally rang, she shrieked and ran for her shoes.

passage: At the kindergarten in Pune, snack time was at eleven, and by ten Sonali was already at the door. "Is it snack time? Is it now? Now?" When Rehana-ma'am said "Not yet," she flopped onto the mat and cried. Rehana-ma'am brought out the big sand timer. "When the sand runs out, it's snack time. Can you help me watch it?" She added a finger game, "five little mangoes", to sing while the sand fell. Sonali watched, sniffing, then singing. When the last grains slipped through, she jumped up. "It's done! Snack!"

passage:
First week of June: Mridul wanted the cricket bat in the sports-shop window. It cost more than he had. He almost spent his pocket money on ice cream as usual, but put it in a steel tin instead. His sister Jaya drew him a chart with twelve boxes.
Middle of July: His friends bought chips after school. Mridul watched, stomach growling, and coloured in another box that evening. Some days it felt endless.
First Sunday of September: The tin was full. At the shop he held the bat, the real one, not the cheap plastic one he could have bought in June. He carried it home under his arm, grinning so wide his cheeks ached.

qa.q: How many boxes did Jaya draw on the chart?
qa.a: Twelve boxes.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel carrying the bat home?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy, grinning so wide his cheeks ached.

qa.q: What helped Mridul keep saving?
qa.a: The steel tin and Jaya's chart, which made his progress visible box by box.

grounding: Shows over months a child saving pocket money instead of spending it, and the pride of getting something better by waiting.

passage: Sumit, you want everything today. Let me tell you about my red bicycle. When I was ten, in Nagpur, I saw it in Gupta-uncle's shop and wanted it so badly I dreamt about it. My father said, "Save, and I'll add the same." So every coin from Diwali, every coin from my aunts, went into a clay pot. My brother bought kites and sweets and laughed at me. Twice I nearly broke the pot for a film ticket. I, Vasudha, held on for fourteen months. When we finally carried that bicycle home, my brother asked for a ride, and I let him, grandly, like a queen. I've never been so proud of anything I owned.

qa.q: How long did young Vasudha save?
qa.a: Fourteen months.

qa.q: How did young Vasudha feel when the bicycle came home?
qa.a: She felt deeply proud, letting her brother ride grandly, like a queen.

qa.q: What was the hardest choice in the story?
qa.a: Not breaking the pot for a film ticket, twice, which kept the bigger goal alive.

qa.q: How might the brother have felt asking for a ride?

grounding: Shows a child learning to delay reward by saving for a bicycle and taking pride in having managed it.

passage: The queue for the giant wheel at the Durga Puja fair was forty minutes long, the evening was sticky, and Anirban's feet hurt. Right beside it, the toy train had no queue at all. "Let's just go on the train," said his friend Siddharth, tugging his sleeve. Anirban looked up at the wheel's lights turning slowly against the dark. Last year he'd have given up. This year he'd waited his turn at the pani-puri stall without once whining, and his mother had noticed. "I'm staying," he said. He and Siddharth played word games to pass the time. When they reached the top of the wheel, the whole fair glittering below, Anirban felt a proud warmth. "Worth it," he whispered.

qa.q: How long was the queue for the giant wheel?

qa.q: How did Anirban feel at the top of the wheel?

passage: At the community centre gym, Akash stared at the mirror after two weeks of push-ups and saw the same skinny arms. "This is pointless," he told Coach Vaibhav, dropping the dumbbell. "The guys online got huge in a month." Vaibhav didn't argue. He pulled out the logbook Akash had filled in on his first day. "Read me your first entry." "Eight push-ups." "And today?" Akash checked. "Nineteen." "Compare yourself to you, not to those videos," Vaibhav said. "Small steps add up. See me in three months." Akash looked at the two numbers for a long time. Then he picked the dumbbell up again.

qa.a: Eight push-ups.

qa.q: How did Akash feel after two weeks?

passage:
Dear Kishore-bhaiya,
You gave me your old guitar last Diwali and said, "Give it a year." I nearly didn't. For the first month my fingers hurt, the chords buzzed, and every video made it look easy. I shoved the guitar under my bed in March. Then last week I found the voice recording I made on the first day, trying to play "Happy Birthday". It was terrible! I recorded the same song again. It's not great, but it's a song now. I'd been comparing myself to people who've played for ten years, not to me in January. So it's back out from under the bed. Fifteen minutes a day. I'll play for you when you're home in May.
Jagdish

passage: Okay, so when I moved to this school in Class 9, I expected to have a best friend in a week. That's how it looks in films. I'm Divyansh, and by the third week I was eating lunch alone and telling my mum I wanted to switch schools. My cousin said, "Make a list of one small thing each week." So I did. Week four: I said hi to Kiran at the bus stop. Week six: we talked about cricket. Week nine: Kiran saved me a seat. It's been five months now. Looking back at that list, I can actually see it happen, slowly. If I'd quit in week three, I'd have missed all of it.

qa.q: What did Kiran do in week nine?
qa.a: Kiran saved Divyansh a seat.

qa.q: How was Divyansh feeling in the third week?

qa.a: Kiran may have felt friendly and curious about the new classmate.

passage: I'm Ira, and I live across the landing from Vidya, so on Sunday afternoons I can hear her teaching her father to use his new phone. Every week it's the same lesson. "Appa, the green button is to answer." He forgets. He gets cross. Once I heard him say, "I'm too old, leave it." Vidya didn't raise her voice, not once in two months. She wrote the steps on a card in big letters and taped it to the back of the phone. She told him, "We'll do one thing a week. This week, just answering." I don't know how she stays so calm; maybe she's fuming inside. But last Sunday, through the door, I heard her father say, triumphant, "Vidya! I sent you a photo!"

qa.q: What did Vidya tape to the back of the phone?
qa.a: A card with the steps in big letters.

qa.q: What might Vidya be feeling during these lessons?
qa.a: Vidya seems calm and patient, though Ira wonders if she is quietly frustrated inside.

qa.q: What made Vidya's teaching work?
qa.a: Staying calm, writing the steps down and teaching one thing a week at her father's pace.

qa.q: How does Vidya's father feel when he sends the photo?
qa.a: He feels triumphant and proud, after once saying he was too old.

grounding: Shows through a neighbour's eyes an adult choosing a patient, purposeful pace to teach a slow-learning parent.

passage:
Week one: Ojas took his grandfather's pension papers to the district office. The clerk said a signature was missing. Ramesh-dadaji, who had come along, grumbled loudly that Ojas was useless. Ojas breathed and said, "We'll come back on Thursday."
Week three: Another form, another queue. Dadaji refused to sit, then complained his legs hurt. Ojas brought a folding stool and a flask of tea, and chatted with the man in front about cricket.
Week six: The pension was approved. Dadaji said nothing for a while on the auto ride home. Then, gruffly: "You didn't shout even once." Ojas smiled. "Shouting wouldn't have printed the stamp any faster."

qa.q: What did Ojas bring in week three?
qa.a: A folding stool and a flask of tea.

qa.q: How did Ojas seem to feel when Dadaji called him useless?

qa.a: He kept returning with the right forms and planned for comfort, pushing the process forward at a realistic pace.

qa.a: Dadaji seems grudgingly grateful and impressed that Ojas never shouted.

grounding: Shows over weeks a young adult staying calm with a slow process and a difficult relative, choosing pace with purpose.

passage: Raghav, you're getting impatient with the new boy. Let me tell you about Sunil. When I was twenty-five and running my first repair bench in Hyderabad, they gave me an apprentice who couldn't tell a spanner from a screwdriver. He dropped bolts and forgot every step. My boss said, "Just shout, he'll learn faster." I, Farhan, tried shouting for one week. Sunil got slower and started trembling when I came near. So I changed. One task a day. Show him, let him do it, check it, praise what he got right. It took him eight months to strip an engine alone. Eight months. Today he runs the biggest garage in Secunderabad. Patience isn't doing nothing, beta. It's choosing the speed that actually works.

qa.q: How long did Sunil take to strip an engine alone?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: How did young Farhan feel after a week of shouting?
qa.a: Farhan felt uneasy and unhappy, seeing Sunil get slower and tremble whenever Farhan came near.

qa.a: Switching from shouting to one task a day with showing, checking and praise.

qa.q: How might Sunil have felt during the week of shouting?
qa.a: Sunil was likely frightened and anxious, trembling whenever Farhan came near.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning that patience with a slow learner, chosen with purpose, works better than pushing.

passage:
Monday: Mridul's drawing of their dog won a sticker, and he danced round the kitchen, singing. Two hours later his brother Jeevan laughed at his wobbly cycling, and Mridul screamed, slammed the door and cried for an hour.
Wednesday: Jeevan said sorry. Papa sat with Mridul and helped him name it: "You felt embarrassed, then furious." They made a cool-down corner with a cushion and his comic books.
The next Sunday: At the park a boy called Mridul a baby. His fists clenched. He went quiet, walked to the bench and breathed. Then he came back, cheeks red, and said loudly, "That was mean." Afterwards he told Papa, "I was so angry, but I used the bench."

qa.q: What won a sticker?

qa.q: What did Mridul feel when Jeevan laughed at his cycling?

passage: Tushar, beta, you remind me of myself. At nine I loved my goat Moti so fiercely I slept in the shed. When the boys at school teased me about it, I cried so loudly the headmaster came out. I'd rage for hours, bang the door, refuse dinner. My father said, "Stop this drama." That only made it worse. But my mother would sit on the step and say, "Your heart is big, Akash. Big hearts feel big storms." She taught me to walk to the neem tree and count its branches until the storm got smaller. I, Akash, still feel everything strongly. But now I call it passion. It's why I became a vet.

qa.q: What was the goat's name?
qa.a: Moti.

qa.q: How did young Akash feel when the boys teased Akash about Moti?
qa.a: Akash felt crushed and furious, crying loudly and raging for hours.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: The mother naming Akash's big heart and teaching a way to count the neem tree's branches until the storm passed.

qa.q: How did the father's "Stop this drama" affect young Akash?
qa.a: It made the upset worse, because the feelings were dismissed instead of understood.

grounding: Shows a child who loves fiercely and has long upsets, helped by a parent who names feelings and teaches a way to cool down.

passage:
Aditi,
I have to tell someone about Tuesday, and you're the only one who won't laugh. Morning: Imran smiled at me in the corridor, and I was floating till second period. Then in chemistry Ma'am blamed me for the beaker that Saira broke, and I was so angry I shook. I nearly screamed at her. By evening I was crying on my bed over nothing: a song, the rain, I don't even know. Ammi came and sat with me, didn't ask anything, just rubbed my back. She said she used to feel like a weather report too at fifteen. It helped. Do you ever feel like this? Tell me I'm not the only one.
Hafsa

qa.q: Who broke the beaker?
qa.a: Saira.

qa.q: How did Hafsa's feelings change through Tuesday?
qa.a: Hafsa went from floating with joy to shaking with anger to crying with sadness, all in one day.

qa.q: What did Ammi do that helped?
qa.a: She sat with Hafsa, rubbed her back without questioning and said she had felt the same at that age.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel receiving this letter?
qa.a: Aditi would probably feel trusted and close, and may recognise the same highs and lows.

grounding: Shows a teen swinging from a crush to rage to sadness in one day, steadied by a calm parent.

passage: Honestly, being fifteen is exhausting. I'm Anand, and last Saturday alone I went from the best morning of my life, scoring in the inter-school final, to wanting to punch a wall at lunch because the ref gave a stupid penalty against us, to lying on the bathroom floor at night feeling like nothing mattered. All in one day. Coach Joseph found me in the changing room after lunch, fists clenched. He didn't tell me to calm down. He just stood with me and said, "That call was unfair. You're allowed to be furious. Just not at the wall." That night I told my dad about the bathroom floor. He sat with me for a long time and said we'd keep talking, and if the low days kept coming, we'd see the school counsellor together.

qa.q: What made Anand want to punch a wall?
qa.a: The ref gave a stupid penalty against the team.

qa.q: How did Anand feel that night?
qa.a: Anand felt low, as if nothing mattered, after a day of joy and rage.

qa.q: What did Coach Joseph and Anand's dad do that helped?
qa.a: The coach named the unfairness and set a limit on hitting; the dad sat with Anand that night and planned to see the counsellor if the lows continued.

qa.q: What is it like for Anand's dad to hear about the bathroom floor?
qa.a: He is likely worried and caring, choosing to stay close and keep talking.

grounding: Shows a teen with intense highs and lows in one day, supported by steady adults who stay close.

passage:
Monday: Hemant came home grinning because Lavanya had laughed at his joke. He blasted music and helped cook dinner.
Tuesday: The class trip was cancelled because of a few boys' behaviour, and Hemant raged at the unfairness, slammed his door and told his mother, Vasudha, that she didn't understand anything. She said calmly, "I'll be in the kitchen when you're ready."
Thursday: He barely spoke, lying on his bed with red eyes, saying he felt sad for no reason. Vasudha sat on the floor beside the bed and stayed. "Big feelings at your age are normal. And I'm here for all of them." Later he came out and asked for chai.

qa.q: Why was the class trip cancelled?
qa.a: Because of a few boys' behaviour.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel on Thursday?
qa.a: He felt sad for no clear reason, lying quietly with red eyes.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do that kept Hemant connected?
qa.a: She stayed calm, gave him space when angry and sat with him when sad, telling him she was there for all of it.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel when Hemant says she doesn't understand anything?
qa.a: Vasudha is probably stung, but she stays calm and keeps the door open.

grounding: Shows over a week a teen's intense highs and lows, with a steady parent who stays close.

passage: In their small house in Malerkotla, Yusuf, nineteen, was studying for an exam when Noor, fifteen, came home and hurled her school bag across the room. "I hate that school! I hate everyone!" The bag knocked his books to the floor. Yusuf felt the old heat: she always did this, walked all over everyone. He wanted to shout back. Instead he picked up his books slowly. "You're angry, I get it. But you don't throw things at me." She stormed up to the roof. He let her be. Half an hour later he carried two glasses of lassi up the stairs. She was crying. "Want to tell me?" he asked. She did.

qa.q: What did Yusuf carry up to the roof?
qa.a: Two glasses of lassi.

qa.q: What did Yusuf feel when the bag hit his books?
qa.a: He felt angry and walked over, wanting to shout back.

qa.q: What did Yusuf do that kept the connection with Noor?
qa.a: He set a calm limit on throwing things, gave her space and then offered lassi and a chance to talk.

qa.q: How was Noor feeling by the time Yusuf reached the roof?
qa.a: Noor was sad and crying under the anger, ready to talk.

grounding: Illustrates a sibling facing a teen's outburst who stays calm, holds a limit and reconnects once feelings settle.

passage: When Gabriel said no to the concert in Madrid, fifteen-year-old Omar exploded. "You never let me do anything!" He kicked a kitchen chair across the floor and slammed his bedroom door so hard the glass in the hallway rattled. Gabriel stood in the kitchen of their Lisbon flat, hands shaking. He felt like a punching bag in his own home. He wanted to go and bang on the door. He didn't. He picked up the chair and texted: "I love you. The concert answer is still no. Kicking furniture is not okay. Let's talk after dinner." At eight Omar came out, eyes red. They talked for an hour, and Gabriel listened more than he spoke.

qa.q: What did Omar kick across the floor?
qa.a: A kitchen chair.

qa.q: How did Gabriel feel after the door slammed?
qa.a: He felt shaken and hurt, like a punching bag in his own home.

qa.q: Why was Gabriel's text a wise response?
qa.a: It showed love, kept the limit on the concert and on kicking furniture, and set a time to talk once feelings settled.

qa.q: How might Omar feel coming out at eight?
qa.a: Omar seems upset and tired, red-eyed, but ready to talk.

grounding: Shows a parent facing a teen's outburst who stays calm, holds limits and reconnects after feelings settle.
